vignette:
Bao, an 80-year-old widower, carried the quiet dignity of a man who had seen too much, a shadow cast by his past as a relief worker in a war zone decades ago. Now, in the structured world of data science, he found a precarious sense of order, but the past remained stubbornly present. The traumatic event itself often replayed in his mind like a relentless film, a scene from a besieged village where he had been trapped, unable to intervene as a small group of armed men, ostensibly there to 'maintain order,' engaged in what he could only describe as abhorrent misbehavior towards the local populace. He remembered the suffocating weight of knowing there were no options for him, no way to stop what was happening, his pleas falling on deaf ears. That feeling of entrapment, coupled with the profound moral violation he witnessed, had etched itself into his very being.

These memories were not distant echoes; they felt like they were happening right now, overwhelming him with a visceral sense of reliving the event. Often, he would wake with a jolt, heart pounding, from nightmares that were merely fragmented replays of that specific horror. The dream residue clung to him, making the transition back to the present day a disorienting struggle. He had come to believe that his intense reactions, the way his body would seize up with fear and his mind would race, meant that he was slowly going crazy, a terrifying prospect for a man who prided himself on his intellectual acuity. What frightened him most, however, was a growing fear of his own rage; the powerful, negative emotions of anger and horror that surged through him felt barely contained, and he worried he would not be able to control them, doing something terrible. The world, in his perception, was an inherently dangerous place, a belief reinforced by every news report he inadvertently caught.

This conviction shaped his daily life. His body felt constantly on alert, a perpetual tension in his shoulders and a tightness in his chest, ready to react to danger that might appear from anywhere. Even in the quiet hum of his data science office, Bao found himself constantly scanning his surroundings, his eyes darting from the doorway to the faces of colleagues, assessing every movement, every sound. He would meticulously rehearse what to say before any interaction, whether it was a simple query from a junior analyst or a team meeting, creating intricate scripts in his mind, fearing he might say the wrong thing or appear unprepared in a world he perceived as unforgiving. News reports, especially those detailing conflicts or human rights abuses similar to what he had witnessed, were meticulously avoided. He would actively change channels, close browser tabs, or walk away from conversations in the break room, knowing that even a fleeting image or sound could trigger the vivid, present-tense replays of his own past.

Over the months, these strategies had become deeply ingrained. His colleagues, though respectful of his age and expertise, sometimes found him distant, his rehearsed conversations lacking spontaneity. His constant scanning made him seem distracted during meetings, even when he was fully engaged with the data on screen. The avoidance of news had left him feeling increasingly disconnected from current events, making casual social interactions more challenging and reinforcing a sense of isolation. His irritability, once a rare occurrence, had become more frequent, manifesting as terse replies or abrupt exits from conversations that felt too demanding or unpredictable.

What finally prompted Bao to seek help was a particularly harrowing series of nightmares, leaving him utterly exhausted and convinced he was truly losing his grip. He felt the weight of his 80 years acutely, a profound weariness settling deep in his bones. He came seeking some respite from the relentless film playing in his mind, hoping to quell the fear that he was succumbing to madness, and to find a way to navigate a world that, despite his best efforts, still felt overwhelmingly dangerous.
